problem: Batched on-policy RL for embodied AI faces a tradeoff: synchronous methods (DD-PPO) are slowed by straggler environments, while asynchronous methods (SampleFactory) gain throughput but consume stale near-policy data and lose sample efficiency. Multi-GPU async methods also need manual balancing of learner/simulator GPUs.
motivation: Embodied tasks in photorealistic simulators (GPU rendering, physics) have highly variable per-environment step and episode times, so scaling to billions of steps is bottlenecked by stragglers. A fixed rollout length is an implementation convenience, not a requirement of RL. Faster training also enables studying open questions in mobile manipulation, such as the skill handoff problem.
key_idea: Collect a variable number of steps from each environment (more from fast ones, fewer from slow ones) within a fixed total T×N batch, with no synchronization points, so learning stays on-policy while the straggler effect is removed.
insight: The straggler effect can be removed while staying on-policy by dropping the equal-length-rollout constraint. VER matches SampleFactory's 1-GPU throughput because it does not contend for the GPU between learning and rendering, and the No-VER ablation shows variable rollouts alone give a 30% speedup. Separately, letting skills keep 'unneeded' navigation actions leads to emergent navigation, because early-training drift makes navigation useful and it is retained; this improves Tidy House from 2% to 32%.
method: Environment/inference workers: environment workers step envs and write to CPU shared memory; inference workers use dynamic batching over all outstanding requests (with min/max) and write experience to GPU shared memory, removing action-level stragglers.

Variable Experience Rollout: collect T×N total steps from N envs with no per-env quota, so fast envs contribute more experience and slow ones less; in-flight steps from slow envs carry over to the next rollout.

Mini-batch creation: randomly order the K≥N variable-length sequences (split at rollout and episode boundaries) and fill mini-batches of T×N/B steps, so mini-batch size is constant; batching uses cuDNN PackedSequence.

Learning: PPO with GAE, truncated importance sampling (max 1.0) to correct sampling bias, and a learned minimum-entropy coefficient; no overlap of collection and learning, saving GPU memory and driver contention.

Multi-GPU: decentralized DD-PPO-style AllReduce, with preemption of stragglers chosen by maximizing S/(Time(S)+LT), and preempted rollouts filled with the previous rollout's stale data plus extra PPO epochs.

Rearrangement application: TP-SRL skills (Navigate/Pick/Place/Open/Close) all trained with base-movement actions enabled, ResNet18 (ConvNeXt-inspired) + 2-layer LSTM, joint-velocity arm control and suction grasp, 500M steps per skill on 8 GPUs.

setting.backbone: ResNet18 (halved width, GroupNorm, ConvNeXt tweaks) + 2-layer LSTM policy, trained from scratch with PPO
setting.training_data: RL in simulation: PointNav RGB on HM3D 1.85B steps; ObjectNav RGB-D on MP3D 600M steps; each rearrangement skill 500M steps on ReplicaCAD
setting.observation: Egocentric RGB (PointNav) or RGB-D (ObjectNav), 128x128 depth for the Fetch robot + proprioception + GPS/compass
setting.action_space: Continuous: base linear/angular velocity, arm joint-position deltas, suction gripper toggle (rearrangement); discrete for Habitat 1.0 navigation
setting.privileged: TP-SRL task planner requires oracle knowledge (e.g. open cabinet before picking); the task specifies object start/goal coordinates

numbers_note: Main results are training throughput (SPS) and sample/compute efficiency plus HAB success percentages shown mostly in figures; these are not standard nav benchmark metrics. The ObjectNav/PointNav validation success is only cited as max success (97.4% PointNav, 13.0% ObjectNav for DD-PPO) in a figure caption, so no benchmark entries were recorded.
results: On 8 GPUs VER is 60% faster on PointNav (3065 to 5325 SPS) and 100% faster on ObjectNav (1015 to 2019 SPS) than DD-PPO with similar sample efficiency. On Habitat 2.0 Open Fridge it is 150% faster on 1 GPU (mean 428 vs 174 SPS), matches SampleFactory on 1 GPU, and is 70% faster than it on 8 GPUs (2861 vs 1662). TP-SRL with skill navigation improves Tidy House from 2% to 32%, and TP-SRL without a navigate skill reaches 50% on NavPick and 20% on NavPickNavPlace.
limitations: Designed for GPU-simulation, large-network tasks; for CPU simulation and small networks it may be slower than async methods and more overlap of collection and learning would help.
Prepare Groceries (5%) and Set Table (0%–7.5%) remain essentially unsolved, and emergent navigation is weaker there.
TP-SRL requires oracle task knowledge, and the ReplicaCAD data is limited to US apartments.
